Reference: Blundell, Gowrisankaran and Langer (2020)

Model Setting

The paper quantifies the value of dynamic enforcement, in which regulatory actions depend on a plant's history of past violations and investments, in the enforcement of the US Clean Air Act Amendments (CAAA). The EPA designates repeat or egregious offenders as high priority violators (HPV) and subjects them to more inspections and higher fines. Such escalation mechanisms increase marginal deterrence for repeat violations while avoiding over-fining plants before they have a chance to fix one-time violations, which is valuable when fines are costly to the regulator, when remediation is slow and stochastic, when inspections give imperfect information, and when the regulator cannot contract on heterogeneous plant costs. The authors build a discrete-time dynamic game between a plant and a regulator. The regulator's inspection, violation, fine and status-transition behavior is captured by estimated conditional choice probabilities (CCPs) rather than by an estimated regulator utility function, and plants choose when to invest in pollution abatement. The plant cost parameters are allowed to differ across plants through a nonparametric random coefficients distribution on a fixed grid, estimated by a convex GMM estimator in the spirit of Fox et al. (2011) and Nevo, Turner and Williams (2016). The data are a quarterly panel from EPA's ECHO enforcement database, 2007:I-2013:III, with 2,355,908 plant/quarter observations on 107,705 plants in the seven most polluting NAICS sectors, merged with NEI emissions, AP3 county marginal damages and NAAQS non-attainment status. Counterfactuals that change the state-contingent fine policy show that removing dynamic enforcement would raise pollution damages by 164 percent holding fines constant, or raise fines by 519 percent holding damages constant.

Enforcement Institutions and Data Facts

Enforcement is carried out largely by ten EPA regions and by state agencies, so regions and states differ in budgets and enforcement preferences. All plants are inspected regularly; an inspection or a self-report may uncover a violation, moving the plant into regular violator status, where it faces more inspections and possible fines, and it returns to compliance only once all violations are resolved. Fines combine a gravity component (actual or potential harm, toxicity, sensitivity of the receiving environment, duration, history of noncompliance, ability to pay) and the economic benefit of noncompliance; political pressure, bankruptcy laws and caps limit the EPA's ability to levy large penalties. HPV status, assigned through ten general and five matrix criteria (some explicitly dynamic, such as "chronic or recalcitrant violator"), triggers intense oversight, higher fines and deadlines, and can be exited only after all violations are resolved. Compliance is high: 95.6 percent of plant/quarters are in compliance and 88.4 percent of plants are never out of compliance, while only 4.2 percent ever enter HPV status. Investment, inferred from ECHO resolution codes (94 percent of investments), PSD permits and HPV exits, occurs in 4.9 percent of regular-violator quarters and 17.5 percent of HPV quarters. Investment last quarter raises the probability of returning to compliance by 38 percentage points; an HPV plant that did not invest last quarter stays HPV with certainty, while one that did has a 49 percent chance of moving to compliance, 26 percent of moving to regular violator status and 25 percent of staying HPV. Investments made while in compliance raise subsequent violation rates, so they are treated as economic rather than prophylactic and are not counted. About 30 percent of investments are followed by another within six quarters, versus about 2.3 percent under i.i.d. investment, which motivates random coefficients.

Regulatory State and Timing

Each period ttt is a quarter and the future is discounted at β\betaβ. The regulatory state Ωt\Omega_tΩt​ is known to both players at the start of the period and has six components: EPA region rrr, two-digit NAICS sector nnn, expected gravity bin ggg, depreciated accumulated violations AtA_tAt​, regulatory status sts_tst​, and two quarterly lags of investment:

Ωt=(r, n, g, At, st, Xt−1, Xt−2),st∈{C,R,H}(9.3.2.1)\Omega_t=\left(r,\,n,\,g,\,A_t,\,s_t,\,X_{t-1},\,X_{t-2}\right),\qquad s_t\in\{C,R,H\} \tag{9.3.2.1}Ωt​=(r,n,g,At​,st​,Xt−1​,Xt−2​),st​∈{C,R,H}(9.3.2.1)

Accumulated violations are the sum of violations since the plant last left compliance, depreciated at the quarterly rate δ=0.1\delta=0.1δ=0.1:

Investment occurs at the end of the period, so it cannot affect the current period's outcomes but affects the next two periods through the lags. The next-period state follows deterministically:

Ωt+1=Γ(Ω~t,Xt)=(r, n, g, At+1, s~t, Xt, Xt−1)(9.3.2.4)\Omega_{t+1}=\Gamma(\tilde\Omega_t,X_t)=\left(r,\,n,\,g,\,A_{t+1},\,\tilde s_t,\,X_t,\,X_{t-1}\right) \tag{9.3.2.4}Ωt+1​=Γ(Ω~t​,Xt​)=(r,n,g,At+1​,s~t​,Xt​,Xt−1​)(9.3.2.4)

The key restriction on beliefs is Assumption 1: the signal depends only on the regulatory state, the regulator's inspection CCPs and the inspection decision,

et∼Fe(⋅∣Ωt,I(⋅),Inst)(9.3.2.5)e_t\sim F_e\left(\cdot\mid\Omega_t,\mathcal{I}(\cdot),\mathit{Ins}_t\right) \tag{9.3.2.5}et​∼Fe​(⋅∣Ωt​,I(⋅),Inst​)(9.3.2.5)

This rules out old investments outside the state affecting eee, and, crucially for counterfactuals, implies that a plant at a given state facing a given inspection policy faces the same distribution of violations and transitions under any counterfactual fine policy. Because eee depends on the inspection policy, changing that policy could shift eee in unobservable ways, so counterfactuals change only fines.

Regulator Policy Functions

The regulator's objective is not estimated; its behavior is summarized by reduced-form CCPs that plants use to form expectations (consistent with a Markov perfect equilibrium or with regulator pre-commitment). The CCPs are estimated separately for plants in compliance, regular violators and HPVs, with regressors x(Ω)x(\Omega)x(Ω) that include two investment lags, region, industry and gravity dummies, and (for violators) accumulated violations, plus inspection-by-gravity interactions where they converge. Inspections are a probit:

I(Ω)=Φ(x(Ω)′γI)(9.3.2.6)\mathcal{I}(\Omega)=\Phi\left(x(\Omega)'\gamma^I\right) \tag{9.3.2.6}I(Ω)=Φ(x(Ω)′γI)(9.3.2.6)

The remaining policies condition on the inspection outcome, with (e1,…,e5)(e^1,\dots,e^5)(e1,…,e5) the residuals of their latent indices. Rather than estimating them jointly, the authors estimate the marginal of violations (probit), fines conditional on whether a violation occurred (Tobit), and status transitions conditional on fines and violations (multinomial logit):

Vio(Ω,e1)=1{x(Ω,Ins)′γV+e1>0}Fine(Ω,e2)=max⁡{0,  x(Ω,Ins)′γF+λ Vio+e2}Pr⁡(s~=k∣Ω,Ins,Vio,Fine)=exp⁡(x(Ω,Ins,Vio,Fine)′γkT)∑k′∈{C,R,H}exp⁡(x(Ω,Ins,Vio,Fine)′γk′T)(9.3.2.7)\begin{aligned} \mathit{Vio}(\Omega,e^1)&=\mathbf{1}\left\{x(\Omega,\mathit{Ins})'\gamma^V+e^1>0\right\}\\ \mathit{Fine}(\Omega,e^2)&=\max\left\{0,\;x(\Omega,\mathit{Ins})'\gamma^F+\lambda\,\mathit{Vio}+e^2\right\}\\ \Pr\left(\tilde s=k\mid\Omega,\mathit{Ins},\mathit{Vio},\mathit{Fine}\right)&=\frac{\exp\left(x(\Omega,\mathit{Ins},\mathit{Vio},\mathit{Fine})'\gamma^T_k\right)}{\sum_{k'\in\{C,R,H\}}\exp\left(x(\Omega,\mathit{Ins},\mathit{Vio},\mathit{Fine})'\gamma^T_{k'}\right)} \end{aligned} \tag{9.3.2.7}Vio(Ω,e1)Fine(Ω,e2)Pr(s~=k∣Ω,Ins,Vio,Fine)​=1{x(Ω,Ins)′γV+e1>0}=max{0,x(Ω,Ins)′γF+λVio+e2}=∑k′∈{C,R,H}​exp(x(Ω,Ins,Vio,Fine)′γk′T​)exp(x(Ω,Ins,Vio,Fine)′γkT​)​​(9.3.2.7)

The paper names the estimators (probit, Tobit, multinomial logit) and the conditioning structure; the explicit indices above are a notational summary. Because regions and industries differ in how fines and inspections escalate with status (the correlation between the HPV-to-regular fine ratio and inspection ratio is 0.06 across regions and 0.09 across industries), the costs of fines and inspections can be separated.

Plant Flow Utility

The plant's flow utility from regulatory actions is linear in inspections, violations, fines and HPV designation:

U(Ω,e)=θIIns(Ω)+θVVio(Ω,e1)+θFFine(Ω,e2)+θHHPV(T(Ω,e3,e4,e5))(9.3.2.8)U(\Omega,e)=\theta^I\mathit{Ins}(\Omega)+\theta^V\mathit{Vio}(\Omega,e^1)+\theta^F\mathit{Fine}(\Omega,e^2)+\theta^H\mathit{HPV}\left(T(\Omega,e^3,e^4,e^5)\right) \tag{9.3.2.8}U(Ω,e)=θIIns(Ω)+θVVio(Ω,e1)+θFFine(Ω,e2)+θHHPV(T(Ω,e3,e4,e5))(9.3.2.8)

so plants may bear costs from inspections (for example shutting down a line), additional violations and HPV status (legal work, reputation, watch-list publicity), but not from regular violator status per se. The cost of investment is θX+εXt\theta^X+\varepsilon_{Xt}θX+εXt​, where ε0t\varepsilon_{0t}ε0t​ and ε1t\varepsilon_{1t}ε1t​ are i.i.d. type 1 extreme value shocks known to the plant before it decides; plants in compliance receive only ε0t\varepsilon_{0t}ε0t​ and make no choice. The structural parameters are

θ≡(θI,θV,θF,θH,θX)(9.3.2.9)\theta\equiv\left(\theta^I,\theta^V,\theta^F,\theta^H,\theta^X\right) \tag{9.3.2.9}θ≡(θI,θV,θF,θH,θX)(9.3.2.9)

expected to be negative except for the investment cost θX>0\theta^X>0θX>0. θ\thetaθ is fixed over time for a plant, varies across plants, and is non-contractible: the regulator cannot offer type-specific enforcement contracts. Exit is not modeled; it is captured through the discount factor, and operating profits therefore drop out.

Plant's Dynamic Problem

The paper describes the plant as minimizing the expected discounted sum of regulatory and investment costs; written in utility terms with the logit shocks entering additively, let V(Ω;θ)V(\Omega;\theta)V(Ω;θ) be the value at the start of a period, before inspection. It integrates over the inspection draw and the signal:

and the expected post-enforcement value, with γE\gamma_EγE​ Euler's constant, is the logit inclusive value for violators and the no-choice value for compliant plants:

V~(Ω~;θ)={γE+ln⁡[exp⁡v0(Ω~;θ)+exp⁡v1(Ω~;θ)]if s~∈{R,H}γE+v0(Ω~;θ)if s~=C(9.3.2.12)\tilde V(\tilde\Omega;\theta)=\begin{cases}\gamma_E+\ln\left[\exp v_0(\tilde\Omega;\theta)+\exp v_1(\tilde\Omega;\theta)\right] & \text{if } \tilde s\in\{R,H\}\\ \gamma_E+v_0(\tilde\Omega;\theta) & \text{if } \tilde s=C\end{cases} \tag{9.3.2.12}V~(Ω~;θ)={γE​+ln[expv0​(Ω~;θ)+expv1​(Ω~;θ)]γE​+v0​(Ω~;θ)​if s~∈{R,H}if s~=C​(9.3.2.12)

The plant's investment CCP is therefore logit:

P(Ω~;θ)=Pr⁡(X=1∣Ω~;θ)=exp⁡v1(Ω~;θ)exp⁡v0(Ω~;θ)+exp⁡v1(Ω~;θ)(9.3.2.13)P(\tilde\Omega;\theta)=\Pr\left(X=1\mid\tilde\Omega;\theta\right)=\frac{\exp v_1(\tilde\Omega;\theta)}{\exp v_0(\tilde\Omega;\theta)+\exp v_1(\tilde\Omega;\theta)} \tag{9.3.2.13}P(Ω~;θ)=Pr(X=1∣Ω~;θ)=expv0​(Ω~;θ)+expv1​(Ω~;θ)expv1​(Ω~;θ)​(9.3.2.13)

Investment trades a sure cost today for a higher probability of returning to compliance over the next two quarters, and hence for lower expected future inspections, violations, fines and HPV costs; a plant in regular or HPV status invests to reduce its present discounted value of future regulatory costs. The discount factor is fixed at β=0.951/4\beta=0.95^{1/4}β=0.951/4 per quarter, which combines quarterly time discounting of 0.0098 and the observed quarterly exit probability of 0.0031.

Random Coefficients and GMM Estimation

Each plant draws θ\thetaθ once from a discrete distribution on a large fixed grid (θ1,…,θJ)(\theta_1,\dots,\theta_J)(θ1​,…,θJ​), and the parameters estimated are the grid weights η≡(η1,…,ηJ)\eta\equiv(\eta_1,\dots,\eta_J)η≡(η1​,…,ηJ​), constrained only to be probabilities:

Since plants are not observed from inception, the state is split into fixed components Ω~1=(r,n,g)\tilde\Omega_1=(r,n,g)Ω~1​=(r,n,g) and time-varying components Ω~2\tilde\Omega_2Ω~2​ (status, lagged accumulated violations, current violation, lagged investments), and Assumption 2 states that observed plants are at the steady-state distribution of Ω~2\tilde\Omega_2Ω~2​ given Ω~1\tilde\Omega_1Ω~1​. Three sets of moments follow Nevo, Turner and Williams (2016): the steady-state share of plants at each time-varying state given the fixed state; that share times the share investing there; and, using the panel, the second-set moment times the sum of investments over the following six quarters, which targets the serial correlation of investment:

The paper describes these moment sets in words; the formulas are a faithful transcription. Inference uses a plant-level bootstrap. A homogeneous-coefficient benchmark is estimated by quasi-maximum likelihood, "quasi" because the regulator CCPs are first-stage estimates.

Identification

In a two-parameter homogeneous model with costly investment and fines only and no shocks, a violator invests when the investment cost relative to the fine coefficient is below the expected reduction in discounted future fines:

X=1  ⟺  θX−θF<E[∑τ≥1βτFinet+τ | Xt=0]−E[∑τ≥1βτFinet+τ | Xt=1](9.3.2.19)X=1\iff\frac{\theta^X}{-\theta^F}<\mathbb{E}\left[\sum_{\tau\geq 1}\beta^{\tau}\mathit{Fine}_{t+\tau}\,\middle|\,X_t=0\right]-\mathbb{E}\left[\sum_{\tau\geq 1}\beta^{\tau}\mathit{Fine}_{t+\tau}\,\middle|\,X_t=1\right] \tag{9.3.2.19}X=1⟺−θFθX​<E[τ≥1∑​βτFinet+τ​​Xt​=0]−E[τ≥1∑​βτFinet+τ​​Xt​=1](9.3.2.19)

so the ratio is identified by the lowest expected fine reduction at which plants invest, and adding logit shocks identifies the scale from how steeply the investment probability rises with that reduction. With four regulatory cost dimensions, identification requires independent variation in how investment shifts expected future inspections, violations, fines and HPV status; some comes from Ω~2\tilde\Omega_2Ω~2​, but cross-region, industry and gravity variation in Ω~1\tilde\Omega_1Ω~1​ is especially helpful. This requires that plants have no private information on future regulatory actions beyond the estimated CCPs. The distribution of θ\thetaθ is identified by persistence beyond what the Markov structure with a single θ\thetaθ explains: repeated investment by some plants and rare investment by others in the same state, more mass at extreme states (many plants in HPV and many in compliance), and the serial correlation targeted by the third moment set. Because leaving compliance does not depend on θ\thetaθ, the distribution is identified from plants out of compliance.

Key Estimates

Quasi-likelihood estimates (standard errors in parentheses) are −θX=−2.872-\theta^X=-2.872−θX=−2.872 (0.041), θI=−0.049\theta^I=-0.049θI=−0.049 (0.049), θV=−0.077\theta^V=-0.077θV=−0.077 (0.197), θF=−5.980\theta^F=-5.980θF=−5.980 (1.005) per million dollars, and θH=−0.065\theta^H=-0.065θH=−0.065 (0.015): all actions are costly, significantly so for investment, fines and HPV. The GMM random coefficients put nearly 98 percent of mass on six grid points with weights 0.438, 0.174, 0.170, 0.126, 0.049 and 0.019. Utility is converted to fine-equivalent dollars by dividing by the fine coefficient:

fine equivalent of action a=θaθF×106 dollars,a∈{I,V,H};fine equivalent of investment=−θXθF×106 dollars(9.3.2.20)\text{fine equivalent of action }a=\frac{\theta^a}{\theta^F}\times 10^6\text{ dollars},\quad a\in\{I,V,H\};\qquad\text{fine equivalent of investment}=\frac{-\theta^X}{\theta^F}\times 10^6\text{ dollars} \tag{9.3.2.20}fine equivalent of action a=θFθa​×106 dollars,a∈{I,V,H};fine equivalent of investment=θF−θX​×106 dollars(9.3.2.20)

For the modal type (44 percent; −θX=−2.334-\theta^X=-2.334−θX=−2.334, θI=−0.194\theta^I=-0.194θI=−0.194, θV=0.143\theta^V=0.143θV=0.143, θF=−5.181\theta^F=-5.181θF=−5.181, θH=−0.029\theta^H=-0.029θH=−0.029) an investment costs as much as a 450,000 dollar fine, HPV status as a 5,600 dollar fine per quarter, and an inspection as a 37,400 dollar fine, while violations slightly raise utility. The second type (17 percent) has lower investment costs (218,300 dollars) and higher HPV costs (38,500 dollars per quarter) and finds inspections beneficial; across the five largest types (95.7 percent of plants), those with the highest HPV and lowest investment costs are those that like inspections. A 1.9 percent type has a small benefit of investment (−θX=0.153-\theta^X=0.153−θX=0.153, a −20,300-20,300−20,300 dollar fine equivalent) and very large costs of inspections (330,000 dollars), violations (266,600 dollars) and HPV status (323,900 dollars per quarter). Among the top five types, investment costs range from 218,000 to 450,000 dollars, whereas HPV costs range from −9,300-9,300−9,300 to 48,600 dollars per quarter, so heterogeneity is larger in enforcement costs than in investment costs. Comparing with Becker (2005)'s 1.1 million dollar average abatement capital outlay implies that a dollar of fines costs the plant about 2.4 dollars; some counterfactuals use 3 dollars.

Counterfactuals

Counterfactuals keep the state-contingent inspection policy, violations and transitions fixed (by Assumption 1), change only the fine policy (and the HPV cost), re-solve each type's dynamic problem, and report long-run means weighted by the observed distribution of fixed states. Because regulator preferences are not recovered, these are plant best responses to alternative policies, not equilibria of a new game. Pollution damages D(Ω)D(\Omega)D(Ω) per plant/quarter are NEI-AP3 mean criteria pollutant damages by regulatory status and fixed state. The baseline matches the data well (compliance 95.11 versus 95.62 percent, HPV 1.42 versus 1.50 percent, inspections 9.41 versus 9.65 percent, damages 1.53 versus 1.65 million dollars). The non-dynamic policies fine all violators identically within each fixed state, never fine compliant plants, and set the HPV cost to zero:

E[Finecf∣Ω]={ϕ(Ω~1)if s∈{R,H}0if s=C,θH=0(9.3.2.21)\mathbb{E}\left[\mathit{Fine}^{cf}\mid\Omega\right]=\begin{cases}\phi(\tilde\Omega_1) & \text{if } s\in\{R,H\}\\ 0 & \text{if } s=C\end{cases},\qquad \theta^H=0 \tag{9.3.2.21}E[Finecf∣Ω]={ϕ(Ω~1​)0​if s∈{R,H}if s=C​,θH=0(9.3.2.21)

with ϕ(Ω~1)\phi(\tilde\Omega_1)ϕ(Ω~1​) chosen either to keep total fines or to keep total pollution damages equal to the baseline within each fixed state. Holding fines constant, the HPV share rises from 1.4 to 30.8 percent, inspections from 9.4 to 20.5 percent, violations from 0.54 to 5.0 percent, while investment falls only from 0.54 to 0.47 percent, and damages rise from 1.5 to 4.0 million dollars per plant/quarter (164 percent). Holding damages constant instead requires mean fines to rise 519 percent, from 320 to 1,980 dollars per plant/quarter (90 percent confidence interval 1,465 to 6,750 dollars), with HPV share 2.8 percent. Doubling HPV fines lowers the HPV share from 1.42 to 1.01 percent and damages from 1.53 to 1.48 million dollars (3.3 percent) while raising fines 13 percent, so further escalation adds little. Effects are larger under random coefficients than under the quasi-likelihood estimates, so heterogeneity with non-contractible types adds to the value of dynamic enforcement.

The second set compares escalation with Pigouvian fines that charge each violator its additional damages relative to compliance, again with no fines in compliance and no HPV cost:

FineP(Ω)=κ[D(Ω)−D(ΩC)]1{s∈{R,H}},κ∈{1,13,1168}(9.3.2.22)\mathit{Fine}^{P}(\Omega)=\kappa\left[D(\Omega)-D(\Omega^{C})\right]\mathbf{1}\{s\in\{R,H\}\},\qquad \kappa\in\left\{1,\tfrac{1}{3},\tfrac{1}{168}\right\} \tag{9.3.2.22}FineP(Ω)=κ[D(Ω)−D(ΩC)]1{s∈{R,H}},κ∈{1,31​,1681​}(9.3.2.22)

where ΩC\Omega^{C}ΩC is the compliant state with the same fixed components, κ=1\kappa=1κ=1 is efficient when the fine cost is purely monetary, κ=1/3\kappa=1/3κ=1/3 when a dollar of fines costs the plant 3 dollars, and κ=1/168\kappa=1/168κ=1/168 restores baseline aggregate damages. Existing fines are about 13 times higher in HPV than in regular status while damages are only 1.7 times higher, so EPA fines escalate much faster than damages. Full Pigouvian fines average 55,240 dollars per plant/quarter (173 times the baseline), cut regular violator status from 3.5 to 1.6 percent but raise HPV from 1.4 to 1.7 percent, and lower damages by 13.7 percent (1.53 to 1.32 million dollars); scaling by one-third gives similar results. This mirrors Mookherjee and Png (1994): dynamic enforcement underdeters one-time violations to raise marginal deterrence for repeat ones. Pigouvian fines scaled to baseline damages raise fines by 394 percent (90 percent confidence interval 445 to 3,950 dollars), the HPV share by 934 percent and inspections by 51 percent, demonstrating the value of escalation. By industry, removing escalation with fines fixed multiplies the HPV share by about 8 for utilities and more than 20 for mining and metal manufacturing; holding damages fixed requires fines to rise 284 percent for utilities but 1,094 percent for mining. Scaled Pigouvian fines reallocate damages away from high-damage utilities, but at the cost of a 561 percent fine increase for utilities, suggesting the EPA finds damage-commensurate fines on utilities costly.

This equation defines the regulatory state Ωt\Omega_tΩt​, the list of everything that the plant and the regulator both know at the start of quarter ttt and that is allowed to shift current and future enforcement. The first three entries are fixed plant characteristics: the EPA region rrr, the two-digit NAICS sector nnn, and the expected gravity bin ggg (five values built from expected actual damages, expected potential damages and county non-attainment). The last four entries evolve over time: depreciated accumulated violations At≥0A_t\geq 0At​≥0, regulatory status sts_tst​ (compliance CCC, regular violator RRR, high priority violator HHH), and the two most recent investment indicators Xt−1,Xt−2∈{0,1}X_{t-1},X_{t-2}\in\{0,1\}Xt−1​,Xt−2​∈{0,1}.

The design choice is a trade-off. The state must be rich enough that the plant's beliefs about inspections, violations, fines and transitions depend on history only through Ωt\Omega_tΩt​ (this is what equation (5) formalizes), yet small enough that the Bellman equation (10) can be solved for every grid point of the random-coefficient distribution. Escalation enters through sts_tst​ and AtA_tAt​: the regulator policies in equations (6) and (7) are estimated separately by status and include AtA_tAt​ for violators. The lags of investment capture slow and stochastic remediation: investment at t−1t-1t−1 or t−2t-2t−2 raises the chance of returning to compliance at ttt. Anything older than two quarters is assumed irrelevant. Fixed components are collected later as Ω~1=(r,n,g)\tilde\Omega_1=(r,n,g)Ω~1​=(r,n,g) and provide the cross-sectional variation used for identification, while the time-varying part has a stationary distribution given by equation (17).

This is the law of motion of depreciated accumulated violations. Here Viot∈{0,1}\mathit{Vio}_t\in\{0,1\}Viot​∈{0,1} is the violation indicator of quarter ttt, δ=0.1\delta=0.1δ=0.1 is the quarterly depreciation rate, and s~t\tilde s_ts~t​ is the status after the regulator's actions in quarter ttt. As long as the plant stays out of compliance, the stock keeps a fraction 1−δ1-\delta1−δ of its past value and adds the new violation; once the plant is back in compliance the stock is wiped out. Solving the recursion backward for a plant that left compliance LLL quarters ago gives a geometrically weighted sum,

At+1=∑ℓ=0L−1(1−δ)ℓ Viot−ℓA_{t+1}=\sum_{\ell=0}^{L-1}(1-\delta)^{\ell}\,\mathit{Vio}_{t-\ell}At+1​=ℓ=0∑L−1​(1−δ)ℓViot−ℓ​

so a violation that is four quarters old counts for 0.94≈0.660.9^{4}\approx 0.660.94≈0.66 of a fresh one, and a plant violating every quarter forever would converge to the upper bound 1/δ=101/\delta=101/δ=10.

The variable is a one-dimensional summary of the history of noncompliance, which the EPA penalty policy lists as a determinant of fines. It makes enforcement escalate within a status, on top of the jump between RRR and HHH: in the regulator policies of equations (6) and (7), AtA_tAt​ raises inspection, violation and fine probabilities. The authors pick δ=0.1\delta=0.1δ=0.1 because it predicts regulator actions better than other rates; it is not estimated jointly with the structural parameters. The reset to zero in compliance means a plant that has resolved all violations starts with a clean slate, which is exactly what gives investment its dynamic payoff in equation (11).

This equation states which part of the compliance signal et=(et1,…,et5)e_t=(e_t^1,\dots,e_t^5)et​=(et1​,…,et5​) drives which regulatory outcome in quarter ttt. The violation indicator Viot∈{0,1}\mathit{Vio}_t\in\{0,1\}Viot​∈{0,1} depends on the state and on et1e_t^1et1​; the fine Finet≥0\mathit{Fine}_t\geq 0Finet​≥0 (in millions of dollars) depends on the state and on et2e_t^2et2​; and the post-enforcement state Ω~t\tilde\Omega_tΩ~t​, in particular the new status s~t∈{C,R,H}\tilde s_t\in\{C,R,H\}s~t​∈{C,R,H}, depends on the state and on the remaining three components through the transition function TTT. All three also depend on the realized inspection Inst\mathit{Ins}_tInst​, which is left implicit here and made explicit in equation (7).

The signal is the model's device for everything that both players observe within the quarter but the econometrician does not: emissions readings, reporting problems, maintenance failures. Its five dimensions may be correlated, so a bad draw can generate a violation, a fine and a move to HPV status together. Two of the functions, the inspection probability and Fine(⋅)\mathit{Fine}(\cdot)Fine(⋅), are choices of the regulator, whereas Vio(⋅)\mathit{Vio}(\cdot)Vio(⋅) and T(⋅)T(\cdot)T(⋅) are pinned down by the signal and by Clean Air Act standards. The outcomes then enter the plant's flow utility in equation (8).

This equation is the deterministic update from the post-enforcement state Ω~t\tilde\Omega_tΩ~t​ and the investment decision Xt∈{0,1}X_t\in\{0,1\}Xt​∈{0,1} to the next start-of-period state. Two features are important. First, there is no randomness in Γ\GammaΓ: all uncertainty in the model arrives through the inspection draw and the signal at the start of the next quarter, so the choice-specific values in equation (11) contain V(Γ(Ω~,X);θ)V(\Gamma(\tilde\Omega,X);\theta)V(Γ(Ω~,X);θ) with no expectation operator. Second, investment has no immediate effect on status or on At+1A_{t+1}At+1​. It only changes the lag entries, and it pays off because the regulator policies in equations (6) and (7) and the signal distribution in equation (5) depend on those entries: the data show that investment last quarter raises the probability of returning to compliance by 38 percentage points. Because XtX_tXt​ stays in the state for exactly two quarters, a single investment shifts the transition probabilities at t+1t+1t+1 and t+2t+2t+2 directly, and all later periods only indirectly through the status and accumulated violations it leaves behind.

This is Assumption 1 of the paper. It says that the distribution FeF_eFe​ of the compliance signal ete_tet​ depends on three objects only: the regulatory state Ωt\Omega_tΩt​, the inspection policy I(⋅)\mathcal{I}(\cdot)I(⋅) as a whole function, and the realized inspection Inst∈{0,1}\mathit{Ins}_t\in\{0,1\}Inst​∈{0,1}. It has three implications.

First, it is a Markov (conditional independence) restriction: given Ωt\Omega_tΩt​, the history before ttt, including investments older than two quarters, carries no additional information about ete_tet​. Nor does the plant's type θ\thetaθ, so the plant has no private information about future regulatory outcomes; otherwise there would be a serially correlated unobserved state and the first-stage policy estimates of equations (6) and (7) would not measure the plant's beliefs.

Second, the fine policy is excluded from the conditioning set. A plant at a given state under a given inspection policy therefore faces the same distribution of violations and status transitions whatever the fine schedule. This is what licenses the counterfactuals in equations (21) and (22), which change fines and re-solve equation (10) while holding FeF_eFe​ fixed.

Third, the inspection policy I(⋅)\mathcal{I}(\cdot)I(⋅) is included. The frequency of inspections may change what signals look like in ways the data cannot reveal, so a counterfactual inspection policy would require a new, unknown FeF_eFe​. That is why no counterfactual changes inspections. The authors note that estimation alone needs less than this assumption: it would suffice that beliefs about violations, fines and transitions depend only on Ωt\Omega_tΩt​ and Inst\mathit{Ins}_tInst​.

As the note says, the explicit indices are a notational summary of estimators that the paper only names. These fitted distributions are the plant's beliefs: they generate the expectation over U(Ω,e)U(\Omega,e)U(Ω,e) and Ω~\tilde\OmegaΩ~ in equation (10) and the transition kernel QjQ_jQj​ in equation (17). The coefficients are identified from how often violations, fines and transitions occur across states and inspection outcomes.

This is the plant's per-quarter payoff from regulatory actions, before any investment cost. It is linear in four outcomes: the inspection indicator Ins∈{0,1}\mathit{Ins}\in\{0,1\}Ins∈{0,1}, the violation indicator Vio∈{0,1}\mathit{Vio}\in\{0,1\}Vio∈{0,1}, the fine Fine≥0\mathit{Fine}\geq 0Fine≥0 measured in millions of dollars, and the indicator HPV(⋅)∈{0,1}\mathit{HPV}(\cdot)\in\{0,1\}HPV(⋅)∈{0,1} that the post-enforcement status is HHH. The coefficients θI,θV,θH\theta^I,\theta^V,\theta^HθI,θV,θH are utils per occurrence (per quarter for HPV status) and θF\theta^FθF is utils per million dollars of fines; all are expected to be negative. Although written as Ins(Ω)\mathit{Ins}(\Omega)Ins(Ω), the inspection term is the realized inspection, a random variable whose probability is given by equation (6).

Several things are deliberately absent. There is no cost of regular violator status as such, so RRR matters only through the higher inspections, violations and fines it brings. Operating profits are absent because exit is not modeled and compliance does not affect the product market in the model. Linearity means the plant is risk neutral over fines, and only expected fines matter in equation (10). Allowing θF\theta^FθF to differ from a pure money metric lets a dollar of fines cost the plant more than a dollar (the estimates imply about 2.4 dollars), and allowing θI,θV,θH\theta^I,\theta^V,\theta^HθI,θV,θH lets non-monetary scrutiny deter. Because utility has no natural unit, magnitudes are reported as ratios to θF\theta^FθF in equation (20). A simple special case, with only θF\theta^FθF and the investment cost non-zero, is the one used for the identification argument in equation (19).

This collects the five structural parameters of a plant. Four multiply regulatory outcomes in the flow utility of equation (8): θI\theta^IθI for an inspection, θV\theta^VθV for a violation, θF\theta^FθF for a million dollars of fines and θH\theta^HθH for a quarter in HPV status. The fifth, θX\theta^XθX, is the mean cost of an investment, which enters the choice-specific value of investing in equation (11) with a minus sign. Hence the sign convention: the four enforcement parameters are expected to be negative, and θX\theta^XθX positive. The paper's results table reports −θX-\theta^X−θX, the utility of investing, so that all five reported numbers are negative when the action is costly.

Three assumptions are attached to θ\thetaθ. It is constant over time for a plant, so persistent differences in behavior are attributed to type. It differs across plants, with a distribution on a fixed grid (θ1,…,θJ)(\theta_1,\dots,\theta_J)(θ1​,…,θJ​) whose weights satisfy equation (14) and are estimated by equation (15). And it is non-contractible: the regulator cannot condition enforcement on θ\thetaθ, only on the regulatory state of equation (1). The last point is central to the economics. With unobserved heterogeneous costs, a history-dependent policy screens plants: those with high investment costs or low enforcement costs linger in violation and reach HPV status, where fines are high, while low-cost plants fix problems early and are never fined heavily. Since the type distribution scale is fixed by the logit shocks, only ratios such as those in equation (20) have a dollar interpretation.

The plant maximizes the expected discounted sum of flow utilities from equation (8) net of investment costs. V(Ω;θ)V(\Omega;\theta)V(Ω;θ) is the value at the very start of a quarter, before the inspection draw, the signal and the investment shocks are realized. The equation follows from taking expectations in the order in which events unfold.

because the exponent form equals I(Ω)\mathcal{I}(\Omega)I(Ω) when Ins=1\mathit{Ins}=1Ins=1 and 1−I(Ω)1-\mathcal{I}(\Omega)1−I(Ω) when Ins=0\mathit{Ins}=0Ins=0.

Step 2 (signal). Given the inspection outcome, the signal is drawn from the distribution in equation (5). Each realization eee determines the violation, the fine and the post-enforcement state through equation (3), hence the flow utility U(Ω,e)U(\Omega,e)U(Ω,e) and the state Ω~=T(Ω,e3,e4,e5)\tilde\Omega=T(\Omega,e^3,e^4,e^5)Ω~=T(Ω,e3,e4,e5) at which the investment decision is taken:

W(Ω,Ins;θ)=∫[U(Ω,e)+Eεmax⁡X{vX(Ω~;θ)+εX}]dFe(e∣Ω,I(⋅),Ins)W(\Omega,\mathit{Ins};\theta)=\int\left[U(\Omega,e)+\mathbb{E}_{\varepsilon}\max_{X}\left\{v_X(\tilde\Omega;\theta)+\varepsilon_X\right\}\right]dF_e\left(e\mid\Omega,\mathcal{I}(\cdot),\mathit{Ins}\right)W(Ω,Ins;θ)=∫[U(Ω,e)+Eε​Xmax​{vX​(Ω~;θ)+εX​}]dFe​(e∣Ω,I(⋅),Ins)

The inner expectation is over the investment shocks, which are independent of eee and are drawn after enforcement; the choice-specific values vXv_XvX​ are those of equation (11).

A remark on the shock convention. The paper states that the cost of investment is θX+εXt\theta^X+\varepsilon_{Xt}θX+εXt​ with type 1 extreme value shocks; the note writes the problem in utility terms with the shock added to the value of each choice. The discount factor is β=0.951/4≈0.987\beta=0.95^{1/4}\approx 0.987β=0.951/4≈0.987, which folds a small exogenous exit probability into time discounting.

The target is the expectation over the investment shocks of the maximized value at the post-enforcement state, V~(Ω~;θ)=Emax⁡X{vX+εX}\tilde V(\tilde\Omega;\theta)=\mathbb{E}\max_X\{v_X+\varepsilon_X\}V~(Ω~;θ)=EmaxX​{vX​+εX​}, where the arguments of vXv_XvX​ from equation (11) are suppressed. These are the only restrictions placed on the estimated parameters. Each plant draws its type once from a discrete distribution with support on a fixed grid (θ1,…,θJ)(\theta_1,\dots,\theta_J)(θ1​,…,θJ​) of candidate values for the vector in equation (9), and ηj\eta_jηj​ is the population share of plants of type θj\theta_jθj​. Being probabilities, the weights must be non-negative and sum to one; the upper bound ηj≤1\eta_j\leq 1ηj​≤1 is implied by those two conditions and is listed only for completeness. The feasible set is the unit simplex of dimension J−1J-1J−1.

What makes this a nonparametric approach is that the grid is large and chosen by the researcher to span plausible values, while the shape of the distribution is left free: no normality, no independence across the five components of θ\thetaθ, and multimodal or skewed distributions are allowed. The cost is that the support points themselves are not estimated. The benefit is computational and is developed in equations (15) and (16): the model needs to be solved only once per grid point, and the weights enter the moments linearly, so estimation is a convex problem over the simplex. Because the constraints are linear inequalities, the solution typically lies on the boundary with most weights exactly zero; in the paper nearly 98 percent of the mass falls on six grid points. A special case is the homogeneous model, in which a single weight equals one.

The estimator chooses the weights to make the moment vector as small as possible in a weighted norm. Here G(η)G(\eta)G(η) stacks the KKK moments of equation (16), WWW is a symmetric positive definite K×KK\times KK×K weighting matrix, and the minimization is over the simplex of equation (14). The two expressions in the equation are consistent once the norm is read as the WWW-weighted norm ∥G∥=(G′WG)1/2\|G\|=(G'WG)^{1/2}∥G∥=(G′WG)1/2: since the square is an increasing transformation on non-negative numbers, minimizing the norm and minimizing its square give the same minimizer.

To see why the problem is convex, stack the data statistics in the K×1K\times 1K×1 vector mdm^dmd and the model statistics in the K×JK\times JK×J matrix MMM with typical element Mkj=mk(θj)M_{kj}=m_k(\theta_j)Mkj​=mk​(θj​). Equation (16) then reads G(η)=md−MηG(\eta)=m^d-M\etaG(η)=md−Mη, and the objective is

G′(η)WG(η)=(md−Mη)′W(md−Mη)=η′M′WMη−2 md′WMη+md′Wmd\begin{aligned} G'(\eta)WG(\eta)&=\left(m^d-M\eta\right)'W\left(m^d-M\eta\right)\\ &=\eta'M'WM\eta-2\,m^{d\prime}WM\eta+m^{d\prime}Wm^d \end{aligned}G′(η)WG(η)​=(md−Mη)′W(md−Mη)=η′M′WMη−2md′WMη+md′Wmd​

which is quadratic in η\etaη. Its Hessian is

∂2 G′WG∂η ∂η′=2M′WM\frac{\partial^2\,G'WG}{\partial\eta\,\partial\eta'}=2M'WM∂η∂η′∂2G′WG​=2M′WM

which is positive semi-definite because z′M′WMz=(Mz)′W(Mz)≥0z'M'WMz=(Mz)'W(Mz)\geq 0z′M′WMz=(Mz)′W(Mz)≥0 for every zzz. A convex quadratic objective with the linear constraints of equation (14) is a quadratic program: every local minimum is global, and standard solvers find it quickly even when JJJ is in the thousands. The expensive step, solving equation (10) for each grid point to fill MMM, is done once beforehand and is trivially parallel.

The Kuhn-Tucker conditions explain the sparsity of the solution. With multiplier μ\muμ on the adding-up constraint, each weight satisfies

[2M′W(Mη∗−md)]j+μ≥0,ηj∗≥0,ηj∗([2M′W(Mη∗−md)]j+μ)=0\left[2M'W\left(M\eta^*-m^d\right)\right]_j+\mu\geq 0,\qquad \eta^*_j\geq 0,\qquad \eta^*_j\left(\left[2M'W\left(M\eta^*-m^d\right)\right]_j+\mu\right)=0[2M′W(Mη∗−md)]j​+μ≥0,ηj∗​≥0,ηj∗​([2M′W(Mη∗−md)]j​+μ)=0

so only grid points whose model statistics help most in closing the remaining gap receive positive weight. The two-step procedure first uses a preliminary WWW, then sets WWW to the inverse of the estimated variance of the moments. Standard errors come from re-sampling plants.

The moment is the gap between a statistic computed in the data, mkdm_k^dmkd​, and its prediction by the model. The content of the equation is that the prediction is linear in the weights, which follows from the mixture structure.

Take a statistic that is a population expectation of some function hkh_khk​ of a plant's observed history, mk=E[hk]m_k=\mathbb{E}[h_k]mk​=E[hk​]. Each plant draws its type independently from the grid with Pr⁡(θ=θj)=ηj\Pr(\theta=\theta_j)=\eta_jPr(θ=θj​)=ηj​, as in equation (14), and conditional on its type the history is generated by the model solved at that grid point, so that E[hk∣θ=θj]=mk(θj)\mathbb{E}[h_k\mid\theta=\theta_j]=m_k(\theta_j)E[hk​∣θ=θj​]=mk​(θj​). The law of total expectation gives

E[hk]=∑j=1JPr⁡(θ=θj) E[hk∣θ=θj]=∑j=1Jηj mk(θj)\mathbb{E}[h_k]=\sum_{j=1}^{J}\Pr(\theta=\theta_j)\,\mathbb{E}\left[h_k\mid\theta=\theta_j\right]=\sum_{j=1}^{J}\eta_j\,m_k(\theta_j)E[hk​]=j=1∑J​Pr(θ=θj​)E[hk​∣θ=θj​]=j=1∑J​ηj​mk​(θj​)

At the true weights the data statistic converges to this expectation, so the population moment condition is E[Gk(η)]=0\mathbb{E}[G_k(\eta)]=0E[Gk​(η)]=0 with

Gk(η)=mkd−∑j=1Jηj mk(θj)G_k(\eta)=m_k^d-\sum_{j=1}^{J}\eta_j\,m_k(\theta_j)Gk​(η)=mkd​−j=1∑J​ηj​mk​(θj​)

Two points deserve emphasis. First, linearity holds only for statistics that are unconditional (joint) frequencies or expectations. A conditional investment rate at a state would be a ratio of two mixtures,

Pr⁡(X=1∣Ω~)=∑jηj πj(Ω~2∣Ω~1) P(Ω~;θj)∑jηj πj(Ω~2∣Ω~1)\Pr\left(X=1\mid\tilde\Omega\right)=\frac{\sum_j\eta_j\,\pi_j(\tilde\Omega_2\mid\tilde\Omega_1)\,P(\tilde\Omega;\theta_j)}{\sum_j\eta_j\,\pi_j(\tilde\Omega_2\mid\tilde\Omega_1)}Pr(X=1∣Ω~)=∑j​ηj​πj​(Ω~2​∣Ω~1​)∑j​ηj​πj​(Ω~2​∣Ω~1​)P(Ω~;θj​)​

which is not linear in η\etaη, because types that invest readily are under-represented at violator states. This is why the second and third moment sets in equation (18) multiply by the state share rather than condition on the state. Second, the weights do not depend on the fixed state Ω~1\tilde\Omega_1Ω~1​: the type draw is assumed independent of region, industry and gravity, so the same η\etaη appears in the moments of every fixed state. Since the functions mk(θj)m_k(\theta_j)mk​(θj​) do not involve η\etaη, they are computed once, which gives the quadratic program of equation (15).

Fix a type jjj and a fixed state Ω~1\tilde\Omega_1Ω~1​. The time-varying part Ω~2\tilde\Omega_2Ω~2​ of the post-enforcement state follows a Markov chain, and the equation is its stationarity condition.

Step 1 (one-quarter kernel). Starting from Ω~=(Ω~1,Ω~2)\tilde\Omega=(\tilde\Omega_1,\tilde\Omega_2)Ω~=(Ω~1​,Ω~2​), the plant invests with the probability in equation (13) (zero if in compliance), the state moves deterministically to Ω′=Γ(Ω~,X)\Omega'=\Gamma(\tilde\Omega,X)Ω′=Γ(Ω~,X) by equation (4), and the regulator's actions then produce the next post-enforcement state. where RRR is the enforcement-stage transition probability implied by equations (5) to (7):

The type enters only through the investment probability; RRR is common to all types.

Step 3 (stationarity). Assumption 2 says observed plants are drawn from the steady state, the distribution that reproduces itself: μt+1=μt≡πj\mu_{t+1}=\mu_t\equiv\pi_jμt+1​=μt​≡πj​. Substituting,

πj(Ω~2′∣Ω~1)=∑Ω~2πj(Ω~2∣Ω~1) Qj(Ω~2′∣Ω~2,Ω~1)\pi_j(\tilde\Omega_2'\mid\tilde\Omega_1)=\sum_{\tilde\Omega_2}\pi_j(\tilde\Omega_2\mid\tilde\Omega_1)\,Q_j\left(\tilde\Omega_2'\mid\tilde\Omega_2,\tilde\Omega_1\right)πj​(Ω~2′​∣Ω~1​)=Ω~2​∑​πj​(Ω~2​∣Ω~1​)Qj​(Ω~2′​∣Ω~2​,Ω~1​)

together with the normalization ∑Ω~2πj(Ω~2∣Ω~1)=1\sum_{\tilde\Omega_2}\pi_j(\tilde\Omega_2\mid\tilde\Omega_1)=1∑Ω~2​​πj​(Ω~2​∣Ω~1​)=1. In matrix form πj′=πj′Qj\pi_j'=\pi_j'Q_jπj′​=πj′​Qj​: the steady state is the left eigenvector of the transition matrix with eigenvalue one, obtained by solving this linear system or by iterating Step 2 to convergence. It is unique when the chain has a single recurrent class, which holds here because compliance can be reached from every state and left from compliance with positive probability. The computation requires accumulated violations to be placed on a finite grid. The assumption fails if plants are still adjusting to a recent regime change.

These are the model statistics mk(θj)m_k(\theta_j)mk​(θj​) that enter equation (16), one of each kind for every post-enforcement state Ω~=(Ω~1,Ω~2)\tilde\Omega=(\tilde\Omega_1,\tilde\Omega_2)Ω~=(Ω~1​,Ω~2​). Each is the expectation, among type-jjj plants with fixed state Ω~1\tilde\Omega_1Ω~1​ observed in steady state, of an indicator-weighted quantity; as explained under equation (16) they are joint rather than conditional so that mixing over types is linear.

First set. The statistic is the share of plant/quarters at the time-varying state Ω~2\tilde\Omega_2Ω~2​. Under Assumption 2 this is the steady-state probability of equation (17):

Each term on the right is computed by pushing the point mass at Γ(Ω~,1)\Gamma(\tilde\Omega,1)Γ(Ω~,1) forward through the enforcement stage and then τ−1\tau-1τ−1 times through the kernel QjQ_jQj​ of equation (17), and averaging the investment probability over the resulting distribution of states.

Why the third set matters: within a type, investment depends on the past only through the state, so repeat investment is limited. In the population, however, the plants observed investing are disproportionately types with low investment cost or high enforcement cost, who will invest again. The mixture therefore generates more repeat investment than any single type, and the data value (about 30 percent of investments followed by another within six quarters) disciplines the dispersion of the weights. The corresponding data statistics mkdm_k^dmkd​ are the sample analogues computed within each fixed state.

So the stated threshold rule relies on an unstated simplification, also implicit in the paper's verbal argument: it ignores the effect of investing today on expected future investment outlays. It is exact if the current decision is the only investment opportunity, and otherwise ΔX\Delta_XΔX​ is typically negative (investing now makes later investment less likely), which lowers the required fine reduction. The identification logic is unaffected: the ratio θX/(−θF)\theta^X/(-\theta^F)θX/(−θF) is pinned down by the smallest fine reduction at which plants invest. With logit shocks the step function becomes the smooth probability of equation (13), Λ(v1−v0)\Lambda(v_1-v_0)Λ(v1​−v0​), and since v1−v0v_1-v_0v1​−v0​ scales with θ\thetaθ, the steepness of the investment probability in ΔF\Delta_FΔF​ identifies the scale of the parameters relative to the unit-variance shocks.

Utility in the model has no natural unit, since its scale is set by the variance of the logit shocks. The fine equivalent of an action is the one-time fine that changes the plant's utility by the same amount as the action. By equation (8), fines enter utility as θFFine\theta^F\mathit{Fine}θFFine with the fine in millions of dollars, so a fine of FFF dollars changes utility by

This defines the non-dynamic counterfactual fine policy that removes escalation. The expected fine no longer depends on the time-varying part of the state: within a fixed state Ω~1=(r,n,g)\tilde\Omega_1=(r,n,g)Ω~1​=(r,n,g) every plant out of compliance, whether a regular violator or an HPV and whatever its accumulated violations and lagged investments, faces the same expected fine ϕ(Ω~1)\phi(\tilde\Omega_1)ϕ(Ω~1​) per quarter, and compliant plants face none. Setting θH=0\theta^H=0θH=0 additionally removes the direct utility cost of HPV designation in equation (8), so that no penalty rises with a plant's record. Inspections, violations and status transitions stay as in equations (5) to (7), which Assumption 1 permits because the fine policy is not an argument of the signal distribution.

The level ϕ(Ω~1)\phi(\tilde\Omega_1)ϕ(Ω~1​) is not a free parameter but solves a fixed-point problem, because plants re-optimize under the new fines through equations (10) to (13) and the steady state of equation (17) changes. In the fines-constant version it solves

ϕ(Ω~1)∑jηj∑Ω~2: s∈{R,H}πjϕ(Ω~2∣Ω~1)=∑jηj∑Ω~2πj0(Ω~2∣Ω~1) E[Fine0∣Ω~]\phi(\tilde\Omega_1)\sum_{j}\eta_j\sum_{\tilde\Omega_2:\,s\in\{R,H\}}\pi_j^{\phi}(\tilde\Omega_2\mid\tilde\Omega_1)=\sum_{j}\eta_j\sum_{\tilde\Omega_2}\pi_j^{0}(\tilde\Omega_2\mid\tilde\Omega_1)\,\mathbb{E}\left[\mathit{Fine}^{0}\mid\tilde\Omega\right]ϕ(Ω~1​)j∑​ηj​Ω~2​:s∈{R,H}∑​πjϕ​(Ω~2​∣Ω~1​)=j∑​ηj​Ω~2​∑​πj0​(Ω~2​∣Ω~1​)E[Fine0∣Ω~]

where the superscript 000 denotes the baseline and πjϕ\pi_j^{\phi}πjϕ​ the steady state under the flat fine. In the damages-constant version the analogous condition equates expected pollution damages DDD to their baseline value. Under linear utility only the expected fine matters to the plant, so specifying the mean is enough.

The economics: a flat fine gives no marginal deterrence against remaining in violation or sliding into HPV status. Holding total fines fixed, the HPV share rises from 1.4 to 30.8 percent and damages by 164 percent; holding damages fixed requires mean fines 519 percent higher.

This defines the Pigouvian counterfactual fine. D(Ω)D(\Omega)D(Ω) is expected criteria-pollutant damages per plant/quarter at state Ω\OmegaΩ (from emissions inventories and county marginal damages, by status and fixed state), and ΩC\Omega^{C}ΩC is the compliant state with the same region, industry and gravity bin. The bracket is therefore the extra damage attributable to being out of compliance; the indicator sets the fine to zero in compliance; and κ\kappaκ scales the schedule. As in equation (21), the direct HPV cost is set to zero, and inspections, violations and transitions are unchanged.

The three values of κ\kappaκ have distinct rationales. With κ=1\kappa=1κ=1 the plant pays exactly the external damage of its status, the textbook Pigouvian prescription, efficient if a dollar of fines costs the plant a dollar. If instead a dollar of fines costs the plant 3 dollars (the estimates of equation (20) suggest about 2.4), the plant internalizes the externality when

3×FineP(Ω)=D(Ω)−D(ΩC)⟹κ=133\times\mathit{Fine}^{P}(\Omega)=D(\Omega)-D(\Omega^{C})\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\kappa=\tfrac{1}{3}3×FineP(Ω)=D(Ω)−D(ΩC)⟹κ=31​

Finally κ=1/168\kappa=1/168κ=1/168 is found numerically as the scale at which long-run mean damages equal the baseline, which allows a like-for-like comparison with the existing policy.

The key contrast with the actual policy is the rate of escalation. Pigouvian fines rise between RRR and HHH only as fast as damages do,

FineP(ΩH)FineP(ΩR)=D(ΩH)−D(ΩC)D(ΩR)−D(ΩC)\frac{\mathit{Fine}^{P}(\Omega^{H})}{\mathit{Fine}^{P}(\Omega^{R})}=\frac{D(\Omega^{H})-D(\Omega^{C})}{D(\Omega^{R})-D(\Omega^{C})}FineP(ΩR)FineP(ΩH)​=D(ΩR)−D(ΩC)D(ΩH)−D(ΩC)​

where ΩH\Omega^{H}ΩH and ΩR\Omega^{R}ΩR denote HPV and regular-violator states with the same fixed components. In the data, damage levels are about 1.7 times higher in HPV than in regular status, while actual fines are about 13 times higher. Full Pigouvian fines cut damages by 13.7 percent but at 173 times baseline fines; scaled to baseline damages they still require 394 percent more fines and raise the HPV share more than tenfold. Escalation thus achieves the same damages with far lower fines, by under-deterring first violations and concentrating deterrence on repeat ones.
